# Fiberwise constant fractional cap covers admit a 2k budget bound

This is a complete restricted fractional cap-cover theorem. It is
stronger than the OC cap-budget constant under its stated constant-
multiplicity premise. An arbitrary overlapping small-cap cover need
not satisfy that premise, so the theorem does not complete OC.

## 1. Statement

Let C be a compact convex set in R^n times R^d, and let
S=C intersect (Z^n times R^d) be nonempty. Suppose q=dim_H(S)>=1.
Let P be the finite set of bases whose fibers K_z have dimension q,
let V_z=H_q(K_z), and let

    mu=H_q restricted to S,       M=sum_{z in P}V_z>0.

Let k be the number of occupied integer parities of P.
Consider finitely many closed ambient halfspaces H_1,...,H_r and
strictly positive coefficients lambda_1,...,lambda_r. Suppose that
for every z in P there is a constant b_z>0 with

    sum_i lambda_i 1_Hi(z,x)=b_z
       for H_q-almost every x in K_z.                (1)

Then at most 2k of these ORIGINAL halfspaces cover every positive
fiber K_z. In particular

    max_i mu(H_i)>=M/(2k).                           (2)

If all cap budgets are equal to D, then D>=M/(2k). Since k<=2^n
and Gamma_d<=1/2 for d>=1, this implies

    max_i mu(H_i)>=Gamma_d M/2^n

within this restricted class of covers. No coefficients are used as
multipliers of the cap budgets in (2); it concerns actual original
halfspace masses.

As a special case, any finite halfspace partition of S up to mu-null
overlaps has a subcover of at most 2k caps. If every cap in that
partition has positive mass, every cap is indispensable, so r<=2k.
This conclusion permits caps containing entire positive fibers.

## 2. Local constant incidence forces a one- or two-cap cover

**Lemma 1.** Let K be a positive-dimensional full-dimensional compact
convex body in an affine Euclidean space. If a positive weighted sum
of finitely many closed-halfspace indicators equals a positive
constant almost everywhere on K, then either one of the halfspaces
contains all K, or two of them have the same cutting hyperplane with
opposite orientations and cover its whole affine space.

**Proof.** If a halfspace captures full volume, it contains K: a point
of K outside that closed halfspace would have a neighborhood whose
intersection with int(K) has positive volume. If there is no such
halfspace, positivity of the constant ensures that some cap has
positive proper volume. Its boundary cuts int(K); denote that plane
by L. On a relatively open part of L intersect int(K), avoid the
boundaries of every other cap whose boundary does not coincide with
L. This is possible because a finite union of lower-dimensional
affine subspaces cannot cover an open subset of L. In dimension one
the plane L is a point and a noncoincident boundary does not meet it.

Choose a small ball about one such point, contained in int(K), that
meets no noncoincident boundary. Every indicator from a noncoincident
cap is constant on this ball. The indicators of caps with boundary L
each jump by plus or minus one when crossing L. The weighted sum on
the two open half-balls must be the same prescribed constant: each
half-ball has positive volume, and the sum is constant there. Hence
the total positive-orientation weight equals the total opposite-
orientation weight. Since the chosen cap has positive weight, there
is an opposite cap with the same boundary. These two halfspaces cover
the whole affine space. QED.

The argument permits multiple caps with the same restricted boundary
and different ambient normals. It does not require a single opposite
pair to work on all fibers.

## 3. Finite occupied-parity Helly, including nonclosed convex sets

We use the following finite lemma: if a finite midpoint-closed lattice
set P occupies k parities, then any finite family of convex sets with
intersection missing P has a subfamily of at most k whose intersection
already misses P. Here midpoint-closed means that the midpoint of
every same-parity pair in P belongs to P.

For completeness, it suffices first to prove this for a finite system
of inequalities a_i.x<=c_i. If it misses P, choose eta>0 so small
that the strict relaxed system a_i.x<c_i+eta still misses P. This is
possible from the positive minimum over p in P of its maximum original
violation. Put beta_i=c_i+eta and choose T_i greater than beta_i and
than every a_i.p for p in P.

Over the compact set of thresholds beta_i<=t_i<=T_i for which the
strict system a_i.x<t_i misses P, maximize sum_i t_i. For every
nonsaturated index i, there must be p_i in P with a_i.p_i=t_i and
a_j.p_i<t_j for all j!=i. Otherwise a small increase of t_i would
preserve exclusion of P, contradicting maximality; finiteness supplies
the necessary positive gap. These contact points are distinct. Two
of the same parity would have a midpoint in P satisfying every strict
inequality, a contradiction. There are therefore at most k
nonsaturated indices. Saturated inequalities are strictly satisfied
by all of P and do not exclude any point. The selected nonsaturated
original inequalities, which are stronger, consequently exclude P.

A polytope family reduces to this inequality statement using finite
halfspace descriptions and grouping each selected inequality with its
original polytope. For arbitrary convex sets E_j, replace each by
conv(E_j intersect P). This is a possibly empty polytope contained
in E_j, and it has exactly the same trace on P as E_j. Applying the
polytope result and then using these equal traces proves the asserted
finite Helly lemma without a closedness assumption on E_j.

For the actual positive-fiber base P in Section 1, the required
midpoint closure holds. The midpoint fiber of two positive q-fibers
contains their Minkowski midpoint, which has affine dimension at
least q. Since the global integer-fiber maximum dimension is q,
that midpoint fiber has dimension exactly q and lies in P. Indeed
the positive base is lattice-complete in its convex hull: the same
argument applies to any integer convex combination, with at least
one positive coefficient. Only midpoint closure is needed below.

## 4. Local-to-global cap-cover lemma

**Lemma 2.** Suppose that at every base z in P some at most t caps
from a fixed finite family cover the entire fiber K_z. Then at most
kt caps from that family cover all those positive fibers at once.

**Proof.** For every nonempty index set J of cardinality at most t,
let

    E_J=proj_base(C intersect intersection_{i in J} H_i^c).

These are convex sets, because the complements are open affine
halfspaces and projection preserves convexity. They need not be
closed; Section 3 deliberately includes that case. By construction,

    z not in E_J  iff  K_z subset union_{i in J}H_i.  (3)

At each z in P a local index set J exists by assumption, so z fails
at least one E_J. Thus the intersection of all E_J misses P. The
finite occupied-parity Helly lemma supplies at most k of these sets
whose intersection already misses P. For every positive base z, one
of their corresponding cap sets covers K_z by (3). The union of the
at most k selected index sets, of total cardinality at most kt,
therefore covers all positive fibers. QED.

This lemma is a statement about ORIGINAL caps and actual fibers of C.
It does not infer a mixed center from a projected center, replace a
sum over integer fibers by an integral, or require rationality of C.

## 5. Proof of the main theorem and the partition corollary

Restrict (1) to each fiber's affine q-plane and apply Lemma 1. It
supplies a local cap cover of size at most two. Lemma 2 yields a
global subcover indexed by I, with |I|<=2k. Lower-dimensional integer
fibers are irrelevant to mu, so

    M<=sum_{i in I}mu(H_i)<=2k max_i mu(H_i).

This proves (2), retaining all positive intrinsic boundary fibers.
Purely integer normals and normals vanishing on a fiber direction
space are included by the full-cap branch of Lemma 1.

A disjoint cap partition satisfies (1) with lambda_i=1 and b_z=1.
If any original positive-mass cap were absent from the subcover, its
positive measure would be disjoint, up to a null set, from every
selected cap. The selected family could not then cover all positive
fibers. Hence every positive original cap is present and r<=2k.
No no-whole-fiber assumption is required for this cardinality bound.

## 6. Sharpness

For n>=0,d>=1, let C=[0,1]^n times K, where K is a full-dimensional
centrally symmetric body centered at zero with volume V. Then k=2^n
and M=kV. For each b in {0,1}^n put

    ell_b(z)=sum_{j:b_j=0}z_j+sum_{j:b_j=1}(1-z_j).

Fix nonzero u and L>max_K|u.x|. The two caps

    u.x-L ell_b(z)>=0,       -u.x-L ell_b(z)>=0

are empty at every other integer base and are opposite half-body cuts
at b. These 2k caps partition the source up to null overlaps, all have
mass V/2=M/(2k), and satisfy (1) with unit weights. Thus both the
subcover size and the budget constant are sharp in the stated class.

## 7. Full ownership destroys the stronger component bound

The earlier proper-partition theorem proves r<=2c(P), where c(P) is
the number of midpoint components, when no cap captures a full fiber.
That stronger assertion is exactly FALSE after full ownership is
allowed, even for intervals and actual midpoint inclusions.

Take n=d=1 with exact integer fibers

    K_-1=[-1,1],       K_0=[-1,5],       K_1=[5,7].

Their convex hull has these fibers, because the midpoint of the two
endpoint intervals is [2,4], contained in K_0. Use four caps:

    H_A={x>=6(z+1)},       H_B={x<=-2(z+1)},
    H_C={x>=1-z},          H_D={x<=1+3z}.

At base -1, only A and B have positive traces, namely [0,1] and
[-1,0]. At base zero, only C and D have positive traces, [1,5] and
[-1,1]. At base one, only C is present, containing the full [5,7].
All exclusions are strict, and the only overlaps are the two cut
endpoints, of zero measure. Thus this is an actual disjoint cap
partition with positive masses (1,1,6,2), total mass ten, and r=4.
Its three bases have k=2 but one midpoint component. Consequently

    r=2k=4>2c(P)=2,

and r>2(k-1) despite |P|>k. This verifies why the projection-Helly
argument replaces pair-label constancy in the general partition case.
It does not claim equal budgets in this particular counterexample.

## 8. Constant fractional incidence need not pair globally

There are nontrivial constant fractional covers in which no two
ambient caps have the same hyperplane with opposite orientations.
Take C=[-1,1] times [-4,4], with bases -1,0,1. Define four affine
thresholds of each kind by

    f(z)=(0, 2z-1, 2z+1, 2z),
    g(z)=(z, z-1, z+1, 3z).

Use the eight caps x>=f_i(z) and x<=g_j(z), each with coefficient
1/4. At z=-1,0,1, respectively, the two threshold multisets both are

    {-3,-2,-1,0},       {-1,0,0,1},       {0,1,2,3}.

Away from these finitely many thresholds their combined unweighted
incidence is exactly four, so their weighted incidence is exactly one
almost everywhere in each fiber. All cuts are proper. Yet the slopes
of the first four thresholds are zero or two, and those of the other
four are one or three. Thus none is a globally coincident opposite
pair. The local cancellation argument in Lemma 1 is genuinely a
fiberwise statement; Lemma 2 supplies a global subcover in the theorem.
This particular example already has a two-cap global subcover:
x>=2z-1 and x<=z+1 cover every base -1<=z<=1. It is not offered as
an example requiring four caps; its purpose is the absence of a
globally coincident opposite pair.

The actual cap masses are (12,15,9,12) for the first four and
(12,9,15,12) for the second four, with M=24. Their coefficient-weighted
sum is 24, confirming the constant-incidence identity. No numerical
search or unproved limiting assertion enters this example.

The independent exact-rational verifier
`../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_fractional_incidence_examples_minkowski.py` checks both printed
examples, including every interval trace, all generic incidence cells,
boundary coverage, the cap masses, and the explicit two-cap subcover.

## 9. What remains outside the theorem

An ordinary positive cap cover has weighted incidence at least one,
but in general it is NOT constant inside each fiber. Three canonical
centroid caps of a triangle give the elementary example: they cover
the triangle, have equal mass 4/9 of its area, and have positive-area
regions of different overlap multiplicities. Products with integer
intervals retain genuine midpoint inclusions and the same obstruction
to constant multiplicity. Thus equal budgets and actual convexity do
not supply premise (1).

Proving the sharp budget bound for every finite small-cap cover would
be a reformulation of the full OC problem, not a consequence established
here. The present theorem isolates and solves the fiberwise-constant
fractional-incidence subclass, and identifies precisely why the earlier
proper-pair proof does not extend verbatim to full-fiber ownership.
